strengths: Clear and practically motivated problem setting: training a weakly-supervised VAD detector with zero real abnormal videos, evaluated on the standard WVAD splits, is a well-defined and valuable contribution distinct from prior pseudo-anomaly works that only supplement real abnormal data (e.g., GV-VAD, Rai et al.).

The proposed pipeline is reasonable and well-motivated: CLIP-based initial image selection with positive/negative query phrases, VLM-based prompt refinement, and I2V diffusion synthesis form a coherent, automatable generation chain; qualitative examples (Figs. 6, 7, 10 including a failure case) and generation-metric ablations (Table 3) support the design choices.

The identified failure mode of synthesized data (inflated feature norms biasing MIL Top-k) is interesting and concretely analyzed (Table 1), and the DARM module (domain alignment + usage-aware memory update) directly targets it; the ablation (Table 5) cleanly disentangles the contributions of generator vs. detector-side components.

Strong empirical results: 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech exceeds the strongest Real/Real WVAD competitor, and 82.5% on UCF-Crime beats the UVAD state of the art under a matched (no-real-abnormal) constraint; Table 6 shows competitive performance with as few as 70 synthetic clips.

Good reproducibility: the supplementary provides full hyperparameters (Table 8), generation settings, VLM instruction prompts, and an honest computational cost analysis (30–55 hours of generation on a single workstation), plus a clearly stated limitation regarding minute-long, context-heavy anomalies on UCF-Crime.
weaknesses: Potential shortcut/memorization concern is not fully addressed: the detector is trained on diffusion-generated clips whose low-level artifacts could serve as spurious discriminative cues. The domain-alignment term only aligns pseudo-Normal vs. real Normal features; there is no analysis (e.g., detecting on real vs. pseudo test features, artifact probes) demonstrating that the learned decision boundary relies on genuine abnormal semantics rather than generator artifacts. Given the very high SHT score, this deserves closer scrutiny.

The setup assumes knowledge of the abnormal class names (and hand-crafted positive/negative CLIP phrases per class) at training time. This is a nontrivial prior not available to UVAD baselines, yet Table 4 positions the method against UVAD methods that use no such semantic supervision. The comparison is fair against WVAD (which uses stronger supervision) but the framing against UVAD should be more carefully qualified.

Reported margins over the strongest baselines are small (+0.6% over CMRL on SHT; +1.9% over MGSTRL on UCF-Crime among UVAD) and no variance, seeds, or significance analysis is provided; run-to-run variability in this regime can be on the order of these differences.

The magnitude-bias motivation is weakened by the evidence: the mean I3D feature norm difference (20.52 vs. 23.03, ~12%) is modest, and the ablation shows domain alignment alone contributes little (96.0→96.8 or less), with most of the gain from the usage-aware update term; the mechanistic story could be better supported.

Only two benchmarks are evaluated; there are no per-class results, no evaluation on open-vocabulary or unseen anomaly categories (a natural strength of the class-name-driven generator), and no empirical comparison against the closest related work, GV-VAD [3], which is only cited.

Writing/typos: recurring article errors ('a Domain-Aligned Regularized Module', 'an initial image'), inconsistent module naming (DARM described variously as memory/regularization module), and Table 6's caption says 'total = 140' while varying counts, which is confusing.

strengths: The problem setting is well-motivated and clearly positioned: training a weakly-supervised VAD detector with no real abnormal videos is a practically relevant goal, and the paper is explicit about the training/evaluation protocol (Table 4 distinguishes data types).

The pipeline is reasonably complete: CLIP-based initial image selection with positive/negative prompts, VLM-based prompt refinement, and a regularized detector (DARM) are each described with sufficient formulation, and ablations (Tables 5–6) disentangle the components.
The paper honestly reports the limitation on UCF-Crime (does not beat Real/Real WVAD SOTA) and includes a failure case analysis (shoplifting), plus computational cost details in the supplementary.
Ablations support the design: usage-aware memory update is shown to be the primary driver of gains, and the clip-count study (Table 6) demonstrates sensitivity to the amount of synthesized data.
weaknesses: Evaluation-protocol mismatch is under-examined. Pseudo-abnormal clips are short, fully-anomalous, and class-labeled, whereas real weakly-supervised abnormal videos are long with only a small anomalous fraction. This changes the MIL bag statistics substantially, and the paper does not analyze how this distribution shift affects the claimed 'fair' comparison; the near-saturated 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech warrants scrutiny (e.g., variance over seeds, per-class breakdown) rather than a +0.6 point claim of surpassing WVAD SOTA.

The margins are very small relative to the claims: +0.6% over CMRL on SHT (the headline claim) and +1.9% over UVAD on UCF-Crime, with no error bars, seeds, or significance testing reported; on UCF-Crime the method does not surpass Real/Real SOTA, so the general claim of 'surpassing strong methods that depend on real abnormal videos' rests on one dataset.

The DARM motivation is somewhat circular: domain alignment is applied to real-Normal vs. pseudo-Normal features, but the actual test-time gap is between pseudo-Abnormal training data and real-Abnormal test data; the mean-norm difference reported in Table 1 (20.52 vs. 23.03) is modest and the causal link to MIL bias is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Generation quality evaluation (Table 3) has no external baselines (e.g., w/o init selection, other diffusion backbones, or T2V vs. I2V), so the contribution of CA-PAG relative to simply prompting a strong off-the-shelf generator is unclear; the KID column is identical across settings (0.03), suggesting limited discriminative power.

Clarity and polish issues: several grammatical errors ('an domain-aligned', 'state-of-the-arts UVAD', 'state-of-the-arts results'), Table 6 states '(total = 140)' while including a 175-clip setting, UR-DMU* is not formally defined, and the supplementary contains internal inconsistencies (e.g., 'Table 8' references in the main text vs. numbering, section '5.1' inside the supplementary).

Only two benchmarks are used; both are surveillance datasets with known saturation on SHT. A third setting (e.g., UBnormal or a synthetic-to-real shift evaluation) would materially strengthen the generalization claim.

No discussion of societal impact or misuse risk: the pipeline intentionally synthesizes realistic violent content (assault, explosion, robbery) from surveillance imagery; an ethics/misuse discussion and safeguards would be expected at a venue of this level.

Reproducibility is partial: key prompts are reported only in Chinese ('Original prompts were written in Chinese before translation'), and the full prompt sets, seed images, and generated clips are not stated to be released, which limits exact replication of the synthesis stage that the results depend on.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem framing: PA-VAD trains a detector without any real abnormal videos while evaluating under the standard weakly-supervised protocol, directly addressing the data-collection bottleneck that limits WVAD deployment. This goes beyond prior pseudo-anomaly work that merely supplements real anomalies.

Strong empirical results: 98.2% AUC on ShanghaiTech (surpassing the strongest Real/Real WVAD competitor by +0.6) and 82.5% on UCF-Crime (+1.9 over the UVAD SOTA under a fair, matched constraint), with a clear component-wise ablation (Table 5) that disentangles init selection, prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware updates.

The DARM analysis is well-motivated and empirically supported: the mean feature-norm comparison (Table 1) gives concrete evidence for the magnitude-bias failure mode, and the usage-aware memory update is identified as the primary driver of gains, which increases confidence in the design rationale.

Good transparency: hyperparameters (Table 8), generation settings, computational cost (30–55 h on a single RTX 6000), and failure cases (e.g., shoplifting) are reported, and the UCF-Crime limitation vs. Real/Real SOTA is honestly discussed.

Comprehensive qualitative evaluation of both the generator (Fig. 7, Fig. 10, Table 7) and the detector (Fig. 8 score traces), plus generation-quality metrics (FVD/FID/KVD/KID) that quantify the prompt-refinement benefit.
weaknesses: Potential protocol leakage concern: the method requires the list of abnormal class names that appear at test time to synthesize class-specific pseudo anomalies. While disclosed, this gives PA-VAD prior knowledge of the test anomaly distribution that UVAD baselines (its main fair comparison) do not use, and the tailored per-class synthesis may partly explain the unusually large jump on SHT (98.2% vs. 85.5% for SeeKer). A per-class AUC breakdown and discussion of this asymmetry are needed.

Missing head-to-head comparison with the most relevant prior work, GV-VAD [3], which also uses video generation for WVAD; the paper motivates PA-VAD against it but never compares empirically under any shared setting.

All detector results are built on a single backbone (UR-DMU); DARM's generality and the framework's sensitivity to the choice of classifier are not demonstrated, and no third dataset is evaluated, limiting claims of generality.
No evidence of statistical robustness: single-run results with no seed variance or significance testing, despite margins of only +0.6 (SHT vs. CMRL) being headline claims.

DARM itself is technically incremental (DANN-style gradient reversal plus a usage-weighted memory update rule); the paper's contribution rests mainly on the system-level demonstration rather than algorithmic novelty, which is acceptable for an applied contribution but weakens the theoretical depth.

Writing issues that should be fixed: 'an Domain-Aligned Regularized Module' (multiple occurrences), VLM refinement instruction is stated to be in the supplementary but is actually written in Chinese (footnote 0) with only an English example given, and the raw-class-label baseline in Table 2 is incompletely specified ('Generate Shoplifting' alone).

Generation metrics in Table 3 lack an external reference point (e.g., FVD of real-vs-real or of raw-class prompts from a T2V baseline), so the absolute quality of the synthesized anomalies is hard to gauge.

strengths: The pseudo-only setting (no real abnormal videos at training) is well-motivated and clearly differentiated from prior pseudo-anomaly works that merely supplement real abnormal data [3,16]; the paper is honest about this distinction and about the supervision asymmetry relative to UVAD.

The empirical finding of a spatiotemporal magnitude bias in pseudo anomalies is a genuinely interesting observation and is well supported: Table 1 shows a mild gap in the frozen backbone, while Table 5b shows it is strongly amplified in the detector space (199.48 vs. 9.13 on SHT), directly implicating MIL Top-k optimization. The DARM design (domain alignment + usage-aware memory update) follows logically from this analysis.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: three standard benchmarks (SHT, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence), ablations that disentangle CA-PAG components (init selection, prompt refinement) from DARM components (DA, update), sensitivity to the number of pseudo clips (Table 6), generation-quality metrics (FVD/FID/KVD/KID), and open-set generalization following the OpenVAD protocol with repeated random splits and std reported.

Ablations support the claimed mechanism: the usage-aware update is shown to be the primary driver of norm correction (Table 5b last two rows) and of AUC gains, and DARM improves results over plain UR-DMU and Sultani classifiers under the same pseudo-only data, suggesting the gains are not backbone-specific.

Clear limitation discussion (UCF-Crime does not beat real-abnormal WVAD SoTA, with a plausible diagnosis about long-horizon, context-heavy anomalies), and the supplementary material provides substantial reproducibility detail: generation settings, hyperparameters per dataset, compute cost, failure cases (shoplifting), and prompt templates.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness across feature extractors is a significant confound. Table 4 compares methods using I3D/CLIP features against PA-VAD with Qwen2.5-VL (3,584-D) features, a far stronger pretrained backbone. Part of the +0.6/+0.9/+1.9 point margins over WVAD/UVAD SoTA may stem from the feature extractor rather than the pseudo-only framework or DARM. A backbone-controlled comparison (e.g., running UR-DMU/CMRL with Qwen2.5-VL features on real abnormal data, or PA-VAD with I3D) is needed to substantiate the headline claims.

The pseudo-only training relies on very large external priors (Wan2.2 I2V diffusion, Qwen3 VLM, CLIP) plus the names of all test anomaly classes. While the paper acknowledges this trade-off, the effective supervision relative to UVAD is not 'label-free' in spirit, and the claim that PA-VAD 'surpasses the UVAD state of the art' should be tempered accordingly.

The scale of synthesized data is very small (140 clips for SHT, 260 for UCF-Crime, 60 for XD) yet yields 98.2% AUC on SHT—above all published results. Given the small SHT test set and no variance/significance reporting for the main benchmark results (std is only given for open-set splits), the robustness of the headline numbers is uncertain; at least three seeds with std for Tables 4 and 5a would strengthen the case.

Some methodological details are under-justified: the domain alignment is applied only to normal streams (justified post-hoc in Sec. 4.3, but not designed for a priori); hyperparameter sensitivity (λ1, λ2, λda, β, τ) is not analyzed; and several key prompts/instructions are only partially described or delegated to the supplement (with one instruction noted as written in Chinese), which slightly hampers reproducibility.

The magnitude-bias narrative, while empirically supported, could conflate generation artifacts with general covariate shift; a baseline that simply ℓ2-normalizes features or re-weights MIL Top-k selection by norm would help isolate how much of DARM's gain is attributable to the specific proposed mechanisms versus trivial magnitude normalization.

Writing has minor issues: Table 5a rows lack explicit labels for the 'Refine-only' configuration, footnote marker 'augmentationl' on page 9, and inconsistent method naming (SF-VAD [5] referenced both as single-frame supervision and CVPR18 citation in Table 7).

strengths: The paper addresses a practically meaningful problem: training a VAD detector with zero real abnormal videos, using diffusion-synthesized pseudo anomalies paired with real normal footage. This 'pseudo-only' framing is a clear step beyond prior work (Cai et al., Rai et al.) that only supplements real anomalies.

The empirical finding of a spatiotemporal magnitude bias in pseudo-anomaly features (Table 1 and especially Table 5b, showing a 20x norm inflation in detector space) is an interesting and well-diagnosed failure mode, and the paper supports it with direct norm measurements rather than only end-to-end AUC.

The experimental package is fairly thorough: three benchmarks, component-level ablations disentangling CLIP init selection, VLM prompt refinement, domain alignment, and usage-aware memory update (Table 5a), a sensitivity study on the number of synthetic clips (Table 6), and open-set generalization tests following the OpenVAD protocol (Tables 8-9).

Limitations are honestly stated (failure to beat WVAD SOTA on UCF-Crime, difficulty synthesizing long-horizon context-heavy anomalies, acknowledged dependence on pretrained generative/VLM priors), and the supplementary provides hyperparameters, prompts, generation settings, and compute costs, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The headline claim of surpassing real-abnormal (Real/Real) WVAD baselines is made under an unequal comparison: PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL 7B features while the strongest baselines (CMRL, UR-DMU) use I3D. The reported margins are small (+0.6 on SHT, +0.9 on XD) and could plausibly be attributable to the much stronger frozen backbone rather than the pseudo-only framework. A UR-DMU detector trained with real anomalies but Qwen2.5-VL features is the missing control that would substantiate the central claim.

The setup implicitly assumes knowledge of the exact anomaly class names at training time (used for CLIP retrieval and prompt refinement). This is a nontrivial supervision signal compared to UVAD, and the paper's characterization of its comparison with UVAD as the 'closest' is somewhat generous; the fairness of the UVAD comparison should be more carefully qualified.

Potential leakage/circularity concern: pseudo anomalies are generated for the exact test anomaly classes, and open-set results where the model transfers to unseen classes, while encouraging, are reported against numbers quoted from prior papers with different feature extractors rather than re-run under matched conditions.

The technical novelty of DARM components is moderate: DANN-based domain alignment and usage-weighted memory updates are relatively standard mechanisms applied to a new data regime. The paper's value rests mostly on the system integration and the empirical bias analysis, which is fine for an applied contribution, but the core regularizer is incrementally novel.

Some analyses rely on very small synthetic-data scales (e.g., 140 pseudo clips for SHT), and the claimed saturation at 175 clips suggests sensitivity to the pseudo-data distribution that is not deeply analyzed (e.g., quality-filtering strategies are not explored).

The paper would benefit from more failure-mode discussion beyond the single shoplifting example, and from a statement on code/data release; without it, exact reproduction of the generation pipeline (CLIP phrases, VLM instruction in Chinese, guidance scales) is only partially verifiable.

strengths: The pseudo-only setting (no real abnormal videos for training) is a well-motivated and practically relevant problem, and the paper positions it clearly against UVAD and WVAD prior work.

The empirical finding of a spatiotemporal magnitude bias in pseudo-anomaly features is interesting and is supported by quantitative evidence (Table 1 frozen backbone, Table 5b detector-space norms showing ~20x inflation that DARM corrects to the real range).

Comprehensive experimental evidence for the claims: three benchmarks (SHT, UCF-Crime, XD-Violence), component-wise ablations of CA-PAG and DARM (Table 5a), sensitivity to the number of pseudo clips (Table 6), generation-quality metrics (Table 3), comparisons with prior pseudo-data and single-frame-supervision methods (Table 7), and open-set generalization with error bars over three splits (Tables 8-9).
The usage-aware memory update is shown to be the primary driver of bias correction, and the DA-vs-Update decomposition in Table 5b gives a mechanistic account rather than only end-to-end numbers.

Honest limitations section: the authors explicitly acknowledge not surpassing WVAD SOTA on UCF-Crime and that supervision is not strictly equal to UVAD due to reliance on pretrained generative/VLM priors. Reproducibility support is reasonable: hyperparameters, generation settings, compute cost, and failure-case examples (shoplifting) are provided in the supplementary.
weaknesses: Feature-backbone confound in the headline comparisons: PA-VAD uses Qwen2.5-VL features while all WVAD baselines use I3D/C3D (Table 4). The claimed +0.6/+0.9 wins over CMRL and UR-DMU may be driven largely by the much stronger frozen backbone rather than the pseudo-only pipeline or DARM. A critical missing control is UR-DMU (or CMRL) trained Real/Real with the same Qwen2.5-VL features; without it, the SOTA-surpassing claim is not fully supported.

DARM components are largely assembled from existing techniques (DANN gradient reversal from Ganin et al., memory banks and MIL scoring from UR-DMU), and CA-PAG is a prompt-engineering pipeline over off-the-shelf CLIP/VLM/Wan2.2 models; the algorithmic novelty per component is modest, with the contribution resting mainly on the empirical bias finding and system integration.

The magnitude-bias analysis is purely empirical; the mechanism by which a mild gap in the frozen backbone (e.g., 20.52 vs 23.03 for I3D) amplifies to a 20x gap in detector space is not analyzed, and it is unclear whether the detector itself, rather than pseudo data alone, inflates the norms. Also the domain-alignment loss operates only on normal streams, which the authors note, but this limits the conceptual completeness of the 'domain-aligned' framing for the abnormal side.

Some evaluation details weaken confidence: the SHT evaluation uses a non-standard revised split of [33] while keeping training abnormal-free, and several strong recent baselines (e.g., VADCLIP, Holmes-VAU) are cited but absent from the comparison table; main results lack variance/error bars (only open-set results report std).

The number of pseudo clips and per-class prompt templates are dataset-tuned (different CFG scales, clip counts, 10-crop augmentation choices), raising questions about how much hand-tuning the pipeline requires for a new domain; a discussion or cross-dataset transfer of the generation configuration would strengthen generality claims.
No statement about releasing code or the synthesized pseudo-anomaly dataset, which limits reproducibility of a paper whose main artifact is a generation pipeline.
